Finding: Every elite clone is a copy of the SAME brain (the all-time-best stash slot), not the top N distinct performers. With the new default of 30 elite clones, 30 bit-identical cars are bred into each generation.
Why it holds the project back: Those 30 cars are deterministic and identical, so they drive the exact same line and produce the exact same fitness. 29 of them are pure wasted compute AND 6% of the population contributes zero search diversity every single generation.
Suggested change: Clone the top N distinct finishers (order[0..N-1]) instead of N copies of one brain, or keep 1-2 copies of the all-time best and fill the rest from distinct ranked parents.
Outcome: Kept as is at your request — ~30 elite clones stop the run forgetting what it has learned

Finding: Crossover is uniform per-weight: each weight is taken from parent 1 or parent 2 at random, independently.
Why it holds the project back: For neural networks this is known to be destructive - it breaks up co-adapted groups of weights that only work together, and two networks that solve the task differently produce a broken child. It is a big part of why progress is noisy between generations.
Suggested change: Switch to node-level crossover (take a hidden unit's whole incoming weight vector from one parent), or drop crossover entirely and rely on mutation, which often outperforms uniform crossover for small nets.

Finding: Mutation magnitude is a fixed uniform +/-0.5 and never anneals. Mutation rate is a flat per-weight probability with no decay over generations.
Why it holds the project back: A perturbation that is right for generation 1 is far too coarse for generation 500 - late training keeps kicking good solutions apart instead of refining them. At the new 30% default, ~30% of every brain is randomly shifted by up to +/-0.5 each generation.
Suggested change: Use a Gaussian perturbation and decay its sigma (and/or the rate) as generations progress, or make the magnitude a setting alongside the rate.
Outcome: Fixed — Gaussian mutation, sigma anneals with generation

Finding: Parent selection picks uniformly at random from the top 20%; the best car and the 100th-best have exactly equal odds.
Why it holds the project back: Throws away most of the fitness signal. Rank-weighted or tournament selection converges noticeably faster for the same population size.
Suggested change: Rank-weighted or small-tournament selection inside the existing pool. Cheap to implement, no data-structure change.

Finding: The network is strictly feedforward with no memory or recurrence - each frame's decision is made from that frame's sensors alone.
Why it holds the project back: The car cannot carry any state (which way the last corner went, whether it is mid-overtake, how long it has been understeering). Limits the ceiling of what these brains can ever learn regardless of how long you train.
Suggested change: Add a small recurrent state (feed the previous hidden activations or previous outputs back in as extra inputs). This is a few lines in feedForward plus a wider IN_N.
Outcome: Fixed — previous outputs fed back as two extra inputs

Finding: Sensor range is hard-coded at 180px regardless of the Max Speed setting.
Why it holds the project back: At Max Speed 25 a car covers 25px per frame, so 180px is barely 7 frames of lookahead - the AI physically cannot see far enough ahead to plan a corner entry at high speed. The high end of the Max Speed slider is effectively unusable for good driving.
Suggested change: Scale sensor length with max speed (e.g. a fixed number of seconds of lookahead), or expose it as a setting.
Outcome: Fixed — sensor reach scales with Max Speed; wall buckets resize with it

Finding: Initial weights are uniform [-1,1] with no fan-in scaling.
Why it holds the project back: For a 9-input tanh layer this pushes many units into saturation from the start, where gradients/where useful variation is smallest. Slows down the first few dozen generations.
Suggested change: Scale initial weights by fan-in (Xavier: roughly +/-sqrt(6/(fan_in+fan_out))).

Finding: Fitness accrues (speed/maxSpeed)*0.1 every frame the car is alive, uncapped.
Why it holds the project back: Rewards time spent alive as well as speed, so a car circling a wide open section of track can farm fitness without making progress. The gate-timing rewards mostly dominate this, but it is still a pull in the wrong direction.
Suggested change: Award distance-along-track rather than raw frames-at-speed, or cap the per-lap contribution of this term.
Outcome: Fixed — speed reward gated on recent gate progress

Finding: Crashing costs -50 fitness; stopping (the new no-momentum rule) costs nothing.
Why it holds the project back: Creates a small incentive to brake to a stop in front of a wall rather than hit it. Worth watching now that braking actually works - if 'suicide-stop' behaviour appears in training, this asymmetry is why.
Suggested change: Either apply a smaller penalty for stopping, or drop the crash penalty and let lost progress be the only cost.
Outcome: Fixed — stopping now costs the same as crashing

Finding: Default Simulation Speed is 1, meaning exactly ONE simulation step per animation frame, each one costing a full postMessage round trip to every worker plus a render-buffer copy.
Why it holds the project back: At the default the app spends almost all of its time on message-passing overhead rather than simulation - the wasm backend is idle between round trips. This is the single biggest reason normal (non-hyper) mode feels slow.
Suggested change: Raise the default to something like 4-8, or decouple simulation rate from render rate (run a fixed-size chunk per frame and draw the latest state).

Finding: Selection sorts the population with an insertion sort - O(n^2).
Why it holds the project back: At the new default of 500 cars that is up to ~125,000 comparisons every generation, on the critical path between generations. It will get worse if the population cap is ever raised.
Suggested change: Swap in a proper O(n log n) sort, or just partial-select the top 20% that is actually used.

Finding: updateUI() and draw() run on every animation frame even when the simulation is paused or nothing has changed.
Why it holds the project back: Burns a full 500-car canvas redraw 60 times a second while the user is just reading the screen or editing settings.
Suggested change: Skip the redraw when paused and nothing moved (dirty flag), as is already done for the stats text.
Outcome: Fixed — 30fps cap, dirty-checked, nothing drawn in hyper mode

Finding: Each car is drawn with save/translate/rotate/scale/4x fillRect/restore - roughly 3,000+ canvas state operations per frame at 500 cars.
Why it holds the project back: Canvas state changes are the expensive part; this is the bulk of per-frame main-thread cost in normal mode.
Suggested change: Pre-render one car sprite to an offscreen canvas and drawImage it with a transform, or batch cars by colour into single paths.
Outcome: Fixed — cached sprite per livery, one drawImage per car

Finding: Every frame is a hard synchronisation barrier: the main thread waits for ALL workers before drawing.
Why it holds the project back: The slowest worker gates every frame, so one busy core stalls the whole simulation. Adds latency proportional to the worst worker, every single step.
Suggested change: Let workers run ahead asynchronously and draw the most recent state each worker reported, or double-buffer so one chunk is computed while the previous is drawn.
Outcome: Fixed — next chunk starts before the repaint

Finding: Each worker allocates a fresh typed array via .slice() for the render buffer every step before transferring it.
Why it holds the project back: 60 allocations per second per worker of up to ~36KB, all of it immediately garbage. Avoidable GC pressure on a hot path.
Suggested change: Keep two preallocated transfer buffers per worker and alternate (the transfer detaches one while the other fills).
Outcome: Fixed — transfer buffers ping-pong between main thread and worker

Finding: Every generation rebuilds 500 car record objects, each with two fresh Float32Arrays, plus a template-string HSL colour per car.
Why it holds the project back: 1,500 allocations and 500 string builds per generation, all discarded next generation. Small next to the sim, but it is pure churn on the main thread at exactly the moment the generation changes.
Suggested change: Reuse the existing car records in place - only the colour and the reset values actually change.
Outcome: Fixed — records reused in place, colours stable per slot

Finding: Called from draw() every frame and does a full .reduce() over all 500 cars to find the fittest.
Why it holds the project back: An O(n) scan 60 times a second to update one telemetry panel. The fittest car changes rarely.
Suggested change: Recompute only when results are applied (once per step), not once per rendered frame.
Outcome: Fixed — picked once per applied round

Finding: Five telemetry bar widths plus a label string are written to the DOM on every animation frame.
Why it holds the project back: Each style.width write can invalidate layout; doing it 60x/sec for bars that move slightly is measurable on weaker hardware, and this file already fixed exactly this class of bug once (lucide.createIcons per frame).
Suggested change: Only write when the rounded value actually changes, like the existing _ui_gen/_ui_alive dirty checks.

Finding: Each sensor result is stored twice - once in car_sensors[] and once in car_in[] - with identical values.
Why it holds the project back: 7 redundant float stores per living car per frame, and ~14KB of duplicated state per instance. car_sensors exists only to draw the spectated car's sensor overlay.
Suggested change: Write once into car_in and have write_render read from there.

Finding: The whole brain array is copied back float-by-float in a scalar loop at the end of every generation.
Why it holds the project back: At 500 cars x 386 floats that is ~193,000 individual float copies per generation where a bulk copy would do.
Suggested change: Use the existing memcpy helper, or swap the brains/brains_next pointers instead of copying at all.
Outcome: Fixed — buffers swapped, only the stash copied

Finding: Eight static scratch arrays of 16,384 floats each = ~512KB of broad-phase scratch per wasm instance, multiplied by (number of workers + 1) instances.
Why it holds the project back: On an 8-core machine that is ~4.6MB of mostly-untouched static memory. Harmless on desktop, wasteful on a phone.
Suggested change: Size the scratch to the actual maximum wall count a track can produce, which is already bounded.

Finding: 399KB of icon library is loaded on every page load to render 23 static icons, exactly once, at startup.
Why it holds the project back: It is the single largest file the page downloads and it draws two dozen small glyphs. The codebase already inlines SVGs elsewhere (SVG_PLAY/SVG_PAUSE) specifically to avoid this library on hot paths - the same reasoning applies to the other 23.
Suggested change: Inline the 23 SVGs at build/author time and delete lucide.min.js entirely. Saves ~399KB per load with no visual change.
Verified: Yes - measured file size, counted icons

Finding: The page loads the Tailwind browser build, which is a full CSS JIT compiler that scans the DOM and generates stylesheets at runtime on every page load.
Why it holds the project back: 407KB download plus real CPU work before the page can paint - on a static site whose classes never change after authoring. This is Tailwind's explicitly not-for-production path.
Suggested change: Generate the CSS once and ship the resulting stylesheet (typically a few KB for a page this size). Saves ~400KB and the startup compile.
Outcome: Fixed — prebuilt stylesheet, tailwind.js deleted (-407KB); screenshots byte-identical

Finding: 208KB charting library for one line chart of two series.
Why it holds the project back: It is 20% of the page weight for a graph that could be ~50 lines of canvas drawing - and the page already owns a canvas renderer.
Suggested change: Draw the fitness chart directly on a small canvas, or switch to a minimal charting library.

Finding: Cache-Control: no-store on the document plus cache: 'no-store' on the wasm fetch means ~1MB of third-party JS and ~48KB of wasm are re-downloaded AND the wasm recompiled on every single load.
Why it holds the project back: Every reload pays full download and compile cost. This was added to fight a stale-deploy problem, but it is a blunt instrument aimed at the wrong layer - it penalises every visit forever to solve a deploy-freshness issue.
Suggested change: Cache assets normally and bust the cache with content-hashed filenames (or a query string tied to the build stamp that already exists in version.json).
Outcome: Fixed — assets versioned by ?v= and cacheable; page itself still no-store

Finding: On every load the app actively clears localStorage, sessionStorage, Cache Storage and unregisters service workers.
Why it holds the project back: Directly fights the project's own goal. The point is to train an AI over a long session, yet a refresh - or an accidental tab close - destroys the trained population, every custom track, and all slider settings. 'Save AI' exports one brain; there is no way to save a population, and custom tracks can only be recovered by pasting generated code into tracks.js.
Suggested change: Keep the storage wipe only for data written by older builds (version-keyed), and persist settings, custom tracks and optionally the population. Solve staleness with hashed asset URLs instead.
Outcome: Fixed — Wipe All Data & Reload button in settings

Finding: The entire zone system (speed / precision / focus / spawnkill, editor UI, per-car-per-frame evaluation in wasm) is used by exactly ZERO of the 25 built-in tracks.
Why it holds the project back: Dead weight in the hot loop (a zone distance check per car per frame), in the editor UI, in the track format, and in the worker message protocol - for a feature nothing ships with and which, because custom tracks do not survive a reload (U1), almost nobody will ever persist.
Suggested change: Either ship built-in tracks that actually use zones and justify the cost, or remove the system. Do not leave it half-alive.
Verified: Yes - grepped tracks.js for zone usage

Finding: The only way to keep training progress is downloading a single best brain as JSON.
Why it holds the project back: Loading it re-seeds the whole population from mutated copies of that one brain, so all the diversity the run built up is thrown away. Resuming a long run is not really possible.
Suggested change: Add population export/import (the brains are already one contiguous Float32Array - it is nearly free).
Outcome: Fixed — Save/Load Session carries the whole population, counters and graph

Finding: Two overlapping speed controls: the Simulation Speed slider (1-10 steps per frame) and Hyper Mode (2,500 steps per chunk, no rendering).
Why it holds the project back: The slider's range is so far below Hyper Mode's that the middle ground is missing, and the relationship between the two is not explained anywhere in the UI.
Suggested change: Make it one control - a speed scale where the top end simply stops rendering - or document the split.

Finding: Initial TTL defaults to 750 and goes up to 10,000 frames.
Why it holds the project back: Now that a car with no momentum is eliminated immediately, TTL only catches cars that ARE moving but not reaching gates. A 10,000-frame TTL lets one such car hold up a whole generation for a very long time.
Suggested change: Lower the maximum, or make TTL reset-on-gate the only mechanism and drop the slider.
Outcome: Fixed — a gate resets TTL in full

Finding: Four exported wasm functions are never called from anywhere - not engine.js, not sim-worker.js, not any test: car_count, get_order, seed_rng, track_width_max.
Why it holds the project back: Dead API surface that still has to be kept working and still ships in the binary.
Suggested change: Delete them, or wire up the ones that were meant to be used.
Verified: Yes - cross-referenced every export against all JS

Finding: The comment '--- Mobile/Desktop Track Editor ---' appears three times in a row.
Why it holds the project back: Pure copy-paste leftover; a reader assumes three sections follow.
Suggested change: Delete two of them.

Finding: Parent index is computed as (int)(rnd01() * poolSize) % poolSize - the modulo can never do anything because rnd01() is always < 1.
Why it holds the project back: Misleading defensive code; suggests the author was unsure of the RNG's range.
Suggested change: Drop the redundant modulo.

Finding: The JS mirror of the physics has to be hand-edited to match wasm/sim.c on every physics change, or the parity test starts failing for the wrong reason.
Why it holds the project back: Two implementations of the same formulas that can silently drift. It already stopped being 'a verbatim copy of the archived JS edition' this session and is now a second thing to maintain.
Suggested change: Either generate it from sim.c, narrow the parity test to geometry only (where the JS side is stable), or accept it and note it as deliberate duplication.
Verified: Yes - changed it by hand this session
Outcome: Fixed — JS physics mirror retired; bench now scalar vs SIMD

Finding: 68 inline event handlers (35 onclick, 17 oninput, 11 onmouseenter, 11 onmouseleave, 5 onchange) hard-wire markup to global function names.
Why it holds the project back: Every rename in script.js has to be mirrored by hand in the HTML with no tooling to catch a miss - a typo fails silently at click time. Also blocks adding a Content-Security-Policy.
Suggested change: Bind listeners in script.js by id/data-attribute at init.
Outcome: Fixed — 82 inline handlers replaced with declarative, eval-free bindings

Finding: The .reduce() that picks the fittest live car seeds the accumulator with cars[0], and the !c.crashed test is only applied to the candidate, not to the seed.
Why it holds the project back: If car 0 is crashed and no living car has higher fitness than it, the function returns a crashed car - the telemetry panel then tracks a wreck.
Suggested change: Seed with the first non-crashed car, or filter before reducing.
Outcome: Fixed — seeded with a live car

Finding: The speed and relative-gate-angle inputs (in[7], in[8]) are only written when relCP is non-null; otherwise the previous frame's values are left in place.
Why it holds the project back: A car with no valid next gate feeds the network stale inputs rather than a defined value. Rare, but it is silent when it happens.
Suggested change: Write explicit zeroes in the else branch.

Finding: The Mutation Rate tooltip still says '15-25% provides excellent exploratory learning' while the default is now 30%.
Why it holds the project back: The UI recommends against its own default.
Suggested change: Update the copy to match the new default (or explain why 30% was chosen).

Finding: README says sim.c is 'about 1200 lines of C'. It is 2,039.
Why it holds the project back: Understates the size of the thing a contributor has to read by ~40%.
Suggested change: Update, or drop the number so it cannot go stale again.

Finding: README's table lists sim.wasm at ~34KB and sim-simd.wasm at ~38KB. Actual: 43KB and 48KB.
Why it holds the project back: Same class of stale hand-maintained number the version scheme was built to eliminate.
Suggested change: Generate these in CI, or drop the exact figures.

Finding: The subtitle line '(Replacement for [TrackML JS](...)' is missing its closing parenthesis.
Why it holds the project back: Renders with a stray '(' on the project's front page.
Suggested change: Add the ')'.

Finding: The Overview says the AI has 'four primary control axes: Gas, Brake, Steer Left, Steer Right'. The network actually has two outputs (steer, throttle), where throttle's sign selects gas vs brake.
Why it holds the project back: Describes an architecture the code does not have - misleading to anyone reading before the code.
Suggested change: Describe it as two analog outputs that map onto four behaviours.

Location: GitHub repo settings (not in the repo)
Finding: GitHub Pages still has a branch-based source pointing at main, running in parallel with the Actions-based deploy.yml. A push to main triggers GitHub's own native Pages build, which republishes main's raw files WITHOUT the generated version.json and clobbers the real deploy.
Why it holds the project back: It silently wiped version.json off the live site during this session and failed the deploy workflow. Any future push to main can do it again - the version display and the deploy-verification job both depend on that file.
Suggested change: Settings > Pages > Build and deployment > Source > GitHub Actions. Requires repo admin; cannot be changed from here.
Outcome: Fixed by the repo owner (Pages source switched to GitHub Actions)

Finding: Every change is pushed to both main and claude/trackml-webassembly-port-rkvuac, which are kept byte-identical.
Why it holds the project back: Doubles every CI run for no benefit, and is what triggers the native Pages build in I1. It also made the version-monotonicity check fail the first time the two branches genuinely diverged.
Suggested change: Pick one branch as the deploy branch and let the other follow (or delete it).
Outcome: In progress — everything pushed to main; deleting the claude/ branch needs the default branch switched first

Finding: verify-live polls the live URL 20 times at 15s intervals - a full 5 minutes of CI wall time before it gives up.
Why it holds the project back: When the deploy is genuinely broken (see I1) every attempt costs 5 minutes before reporting it.
Suggested change: Back off exponentially and fail earlier, or distinguish 'site 404s entirely' (fail fast) from 'site serves an older commit' (keep waiting).
Verified: Yes - read the logs this session

Finding: Playwright plus a Chromium download is installed from scratch on every CI run.
Why it holds the project back: Dominates the test job's wall time; the actual tests take seconds.
Suggested change: Cache the Playwright browser directory between runs with actions/cache.

Finding: Both wasm binaries are committed and CI fails if a rebuild does not reproduce them byte-for-byte.
Why it holds the project back: Justified (Pages serves the repo as-is), but it pins the project to one exact clang version forever - a CI image upgrade that changes codegen will fail the build with a confusing diff rather than a compiler message.
Suggested change: Pin the clang version explicitly in CI so the eventual failure is legible, or build in CI and publish the artifact instead of committing it.
